tip: Use constraints deliberately because restrictions force sharper, more creative card and system design.
sourceTitle: Twenty Years, Twenty Lessons—Part 3

tip: Do not rely on one fixed method or one personal strength because overusing it can turn it into a weakness.
sourceTitle: How Reiner Knizia makes games

tip: Treat luck as uncertainty in outcome, then decide where that uncertainty makes the game more interesting.
sourceTitle: Luck vs Skill with Richard Garfield

tip: Prototype quickly, playtest often, and use notes from real sessions instead of relying on memory.
sourceTitle: Tabletop Game Prototyping, Playtesting, and Development

tip: Minimize unnecessary frustration because tension is useful but avoidable annoyance erodes the experience.
sourceTitle: The Top 10 Things I Learned About Game Design in 2013

tip: Give players small but crucial choices that feel simple to understand and painful to optimize.
sourceTitle: The Art of Design: Interviews to Game Designers #8 – Bruno Cathala

tip: Start by designing a game you would actually want to play yourself.
sourceTitle: The Art of Design: Interviews to Game Designers #8 – Bruno Cathala

tip: Before endless playtesting, try multiple ideas yourself and learn why each failed.
sourceTitle: The Art of Design: Interviews to Game Designers #16 – Uwe Rosenberg

tip: In cooperative games, tune the emotional rhythm so players cycle between hope, fear, recovery, and crisis.
sourceTitle: Games of Emotion: Interview with Game Designer Matt Leacock

tip: Use difficulty options or feedback loops so the challenge can match the players’ skill level.
sourceTitle: Games of Emotion: Interview with Game Designer Matt Leacock

tip: For campaign or legacy games, give players reasons to care about what will happen at the next session.
sourceTitle: Rob Daviau — Innovating Legacy Gameplay, Revitalizing Classics, and Designing a Sequel to Clank

tip: Think of a game as mechanics, flavor, and data, then make sure the card set or component mix supports the core loop.
sourceTitle: The Art of Design: Interviews to Game Designers #19 – Donald X. Vaccarino

tip: Variable setup can preserve replayability when the core action structure is intentionally simple.
sourceTitle: Meaningful Decisions: Donald X. Vaccarino on Design

tip: A distinctive theme can open design space when the mechanics express what is interesting about that subject.
sourceTitle: Interview with Elizabeth Hargrave, Designer of Wingspan and The Fox Experiment

tip: Design for the kind of joy or surprise you want players to feel, not just for mechanical novelty.
sourceTitle: Vlaada Chvátil — Designing for Joy, Building Great Games, and the Magic of Codenames

tip: Design around the player emotion you want, then make every mechanism serve that emotional arc.
sourceTitle: Eric Lang’s Best Advice

tip: Keep the core decision easy to understand, then let replayability come from timing, interaction, and context.
sourceTitle: The Art of Design: Interviews to Game Designers #17 – Antoine Bauza

tip: Let players feel clever by giving them several useful actions, not one obviously correct move.
sourceTitle: The Art of Design: Interviews to Game Designers #10 – Stefan Feld

tip: Use artificial restrictions as a creative tool when a design has too many possible directions.
sourceTitle: The Art of Design: Interviews to Game Designers #12 – Friedemann Friese

tip: A strong co-designer can expose the flaws you are too close to see.
sourceTitle: The Art of Design: Interviews to game designers #7 – Wolfgang Kramer

tip: A funny or chaotic game still needs a disciplined structure underneath the jokes.
sourceTitle: The Art of Design: Interviews to Game Designers #15 – Vlaada Chvatil

tip: Make uncertainty useful by letting players plan around risk instead of merely suffer from randomness.
sourceTitle: The Art of Design: Interviews to Game Designers #20 – Richard Garfield

tip: Trim the design until the game’s central pleasure is visible without explanation.
sourceTitle: The Art of Design: Interviews to Game Designers #13 – Sebastièn Pauchon

tip: Clean mechanisms work best when the game gives players constant pressure to prioritize.
sourceTitle: The Art of Design: Interviews to Game Designers #22 – Rudiger Dorn

tip: Test many internal variations before asking playtesters to solve problems you can already identify yourself.
sourceTitle: The Art of Design: Interviews to Game Designers #16 – Uwe Rosenberg

tip: Separate mechanics, flavor, and data so you can fix the broken part without rewriting the whole game.
sourceTitle: The Art of Design: Interviews to Game Designers #19 – Donald X. Vaccarino

tip: Be ruthless enough to throw away good work when it no longer serves the game.
sourceTitle: How Cole Wehrle Makes Games

tip: In narrative games, let mechanisms reveal story instead of pausing the game to deliver story.
sourceTitle: Designing a Narrative Driven Game with Nikki Valens

tip: Build from a strong experiential hook before polishing subsystems around it.
sourceTitle: The Design Process of Corey Konieczka

tip: Do not start with a theme you do not care about because complexity needs passion to survive development.
sourceTitle: Interview with Vital Lacerda | Cardboard Fire Interviews

tip: For heavy games, design for the second play as much as the first because depth needs room to unfold.
sourceTitle: Be Patient: An Interview With Vital Lacerda

tip: Layer engine-building concepts gradually so players can see how early choices become later momentum.
sourceTitle: Designing Engine-Building Games with Elizabeth Hargrave

tip: Design stories players retell after the game rather than only stories printed in the rulebook.
sourceTitle: Designing Games that Tell Stories with Ignacy Trzewiczek

tip: Cooperative tension works when players can see the crisis coming but still argue over how to stop it.
sourceTitle: Crafting the Player Experience with Matt Leacock

tip: In legacy games, make consequences visible enough that players feel ownership of the changed board.
sourceTitle: How Board Game Designer Rob Daviau Built His Creepiest Game Yet

tip: Prototype the smallest playable version of the core loop before investing in content volume.
sourceTitle: How to Design and Publish Games with Justin Gary

tip: Small component counts force every card to do real work.
sourceTitle: Designing Small Games that Pack a Big Punch with Jason Tagmire

tip: Control scope through abstraction because a literal simulation usually becomes too large to finish.
sourceTitle: Keeping a Design from Getting out of Hand with Gil Hova

tip: Solo games need an opponent system that creates pressure without making the player do accounting.
sourceTitle: How to Design a Solo Game with Hermann Luttmann

tip: Mass-market games need a physical or social hook that people understand before the rules explanation ends.
sourceTitle: How to Design Games for the Mass Market with Leslie Scott and Freddie Scott Vollrath

knownFor: The Tea Dragon Society Card Game
tip: When designing for licensed IP, make the game feel like the property rather than just decorating a mechanism with it.
sourceTitle: Designing Games Based on a Licensed IP with Daryl Andrews

tip: Use app integration only where it reduces friction, hides upkeep, or enables experiences cardboard cannot handle cleanly.
sourceTitle: Mansions of Madness Q&A

tip: Run playtests with a clear question so feedback solves the current design problem instead of becoming noise.
sourceTitle: Carla Kopp on How to Run an Effective Playtest

tip: A game is strongest when the rules are simple but the decisions remain rich.
sourceTitle: Designer Interview: Reiner Knizia

tip: Do not assume every game must be conventionally fun; games can explore discomfort, politics, memory, and grief.
sourceTitle: The Personal, Political Art of Board-Game Design
